556: The biplot presents the same result in graphical form. Treatments lying close together possess a similar quality profile, and a treatment lying near a vector is high in that parameter (Jolliffe, 2002). The twelve treatments separated into three distinct groups along the first component in the order plain, carrot fortified and beet fortified, while the four varieties fell in the same order within every group, namely Dudeshwar, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira. Fortification therefore determined the broad position of a treatment and variety its position within the group, so that fortification constituted the stronger factor and variety the weaker. KBI occupied the extreme positive position, proximate to the phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant and anthocyanin vectors, and DI the extreme negative position, proximate to the starch, carbohydrate and lightness vectors. The two years of each treatment invariably fell close together, most probably because the treatment effects were reproducible across the two seasons, which affords independent support for pooling the data. A comparable application of the method was made by Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026), who subjected twenty seven colour, textural and nutritional attributes of idli to principal component analysis and used the position of the products on the biplot to identify the most promising formulations.
559: Cluster analysis was performed on the standardised values of the forty two parameters of the twelve treatment combinations in order to group the treatments according to their overall quality. The squared Euclidean distance served as the measure of dissimilarity, and the groups were formed by the minimum variance method of Ward (1963), which is widely employed for food quality data on account of the compact, nearly equal groups it yields (Everitt et al., 2011). The dendrogram is given in Fig. 4.46, the composition of the clusters in Table 4.46 and the cluster means in Table 4.47. The cophenetic correlation coefficient was 0.793, which demonstrates that the dendrogram represents the original distance matrix reasonably faithfully (Murtagh and Legendre, 2014).
568: The twelve treatments resolved into four clusters at a linkage distance of approximately 9.4. Cluster I comprised the three plain products of the aromatic landraces, namely GI, KI and RI; Cluster II comprised DI alone; Cluster III comprised all four carrot fortified products and Cluster IV all four beet fortified products. The salient point is that the first division was determined by fortification and not by variety, all four beet fortified treatments grouping together irrespective of parent variety, and the same obtaining for the carrot fortified treatments. This confirms the result of the principal component analysis, namely that the type of fortification constitutes the principal source of variation in product quality. Variety was operative only at the second level, where the plain product of the non-aromatic check separated from the plain products of the three aromatic landraces and formed a cluster of its own. This separation is itself informative, since it demonstrates that the quality of the non-aromatic check departs from that of the aromatic landraces to a greater extent than any two aromatic landraces depart from each other.
569: The cluster means characterise the four groups distinctly. Cluster IV, the beet fortified group, returned the highest total phenol (265.22 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹), total flavonoid (142.75 mg QE 100 g⁻¹), total antioxidant activity (393.44 mg TE 100 g⁻¹), total soluble protein (2.24 per cent), calcium (500.89 mg L⁻¹), anthocyanin (1.41) and overall acceptability (8.06), together with the lowest amylose, starch, total carbohydrate and lightness. Cluster III, the carrot fortified group, was intermediate for the bioactive fractions but returned by far the highest beta-carotene (38.85), the highest resistant starch among the fortified groups (1.69 per cent), the lowest predicted glycaemic index (60.49) and the highest redness (11.57). Cluster I, the plain aromatic group, exhibited high starch, the highest total protein (13.09 per cent), the greatest hardness (114.11) and a moderate acceptability of 7.28. Cluster II, comprising DI alone, returned the highest amylose, starch and total carbohydrate and the lowest total phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant activity and overall acceptability (6.14). On this basis Cluster IV is the group of choice where a functional product of high antioxidant value and high acceptability is required, and Cluster III where a provitamin A-rich product of low glycaemic response is required.
573: The present experiment was undertaken to evaluate the sensory and nutritional quality of idli prepared from three traditional aromatic rice landraces of West Bengal, namely Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira, together with the non-aromatic check Dudeshwar, each employed plain and fortified with carrot or beet extract. The experiment was laid out in a two-factor completely randomised design with three replications and was repeated in two consecutive years, yielding twelve treatment combinations and forty two quality parameters. The salient findings are summarised below.
574: Pooling of the data was justified by the Bartlett chi-square test, which proved non-significant for all but four characters; for manganese, ash, PGI and springiness an Aitken transformation was applied prior to analysis. The experiment was precise, the coefficient of variation remaining below 3 per cent for most characters, with the lowest values for calcium (0.20 per cent) and for total phenol and antioxidant activity (0.34 per cent each). The variety and product interaction was highly significant for the great majority of the nutritional, mineral, colour and textural characters, demonstrating that the four varieties did not respond identically to fortification. It proved non-significant only for taste, texture, appearance, cooking quality and overall acceptability.
575: Among the carbohydrate fractions, amylose ranged from 16.75 per cent in DI to 9.78 per cent in RBI, placing every combination within the low-amylose class. Starch declined from 51.66 per cent in DI to 24.05 per cent in GBI and total carbohydrate from 60.21 to 40.91 per cent, while total soluble sugar rose in the converse direction from 0.53 per cent in RI to 3.83 per cent in RBI. Resistant starch was highest in DCI (1.97 per cent), and the predicted glycaemic index lowest in RCI (58.46) and highest in KBI (75.08), the carrot fortified treatments consistently returning the most favourable glycaemic profile.
576: Among the proximate constituents, total soluble protein ranged from 2.71 per cent in KBI to 1.05 per cent in DI and total protein from 13.44 per cent in KI to 10.92 per cent in DCI, the three aromatic landraces exceeding the non-aromatic check throughout. Fat was uniformly low at 0.17 to 0.28 per cent, as is to be expected of a steamed product. Ash ranged from 5.21 per cent in GBI to 2.47 per cent in DI and phytate from 2.52 mg g⁻¹ in KBI to 0.82 mg g⁻¹ in GI, both being highest in the beet fortified treatments.
577: The bioactive fractions exhibited the widest variation of any group of characters. Total phenol ranged from 290.97 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹ in KBI to 53.47 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹ in DI, a differential exceeding fivefold, and total flavonoid and total antioxidant activity followed the same order, from 171.34 to 42.95 mg QE 100 g⁻¹ and from 426.88 to 165.26 mg TE 100 g⁻¹ respectively. Beta-carotene was contributed almost entirely by carrot, attaining 45.77 in KCI against nil in every plain treatment, while anthocyanin was recorded only in the beet fortified treatments, attaining 1.86 in KBI.
578: Among the minerals, calcium exhibited the greatest response to fortification, rising from 61.44 mg L⁻¹ in KI to 550.88 mg L⁻¹ in GBI. Copper was highest in GBI (0.97 mg L⁻¹), iron and zinc in RI (3.36 and 0.89 mg L⁻¹) and manganese in GI (0.69 mg L⁻¹). Manganese was the only character for which the main effect of fortification proved non-significant.
579: Fortification altered the colour of the product markedly. Lightness declined from 72.92 in DI to 36.47 in DBI, redness rose from -1.81 in DI to 13.26 in DCI, and yellowness declined from 110.98 to 59.45. The total colour difference ranged from 28.70 to 45.02, in every case far above the threshold at which a change becomes visible to an untrained eye. The texture was correspondingly softened, hardness declining from 147.73 in KI to 45.09 in DI, springiness from 1.04 to 0.46, and gumminess and chewiness from 11890.93 and 10263.60 in KI to their lowest values in KBI.
580: On the sensory panel, aroma was scored highest in GI (7.70) and lowest in KCI (5.65), demonstrating that the vegetable extract partly masks the native aroma of the rice. For every other attribute the fortified treatments were superior, overall acceptability ranging from 8.64 in KBI to 6.14 in DI. The non-significant interaction for the principal sensory attributes established that the benefit conferred by fortification was of equal magnitude in all four varieties.
581: The multivariate analyses reinforced these findings. Correlation demonstrated that overall acceptability was governed chiefly by colour and texture, being negatively related to total carbohydrate (r = -0.895) and positively to total flavonoid (r = 0.782). Principal component analysis extracted a first component explaining 50.12 per cent of the variation, which separated the plain, carrot fortified and beet fortified products along a single fortification gradient. Cluster analysis resolved the twelve treatments into four clusters in which the first division was again determined by fortification and not by variety, the plain product of the non-aromatic check standing apart as a cluster of its own.
583: It may be concluded from the present experiment that variety, type of fortification and their interaction all exert a significant influence upon the nutritional, mineral, colour, textural and sensory quality of idli prepared from aromatic rice, and that fortification is the stronger of the two factors. Both the principal component analysis and the cluster analysis identified fortification, rather than variety, as the principal source of variation in product quality, variety operating at a second level within each product group.
584: The three aromatic landraces were superior to the non-aromatic check Dudeshwar for protein, phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant potential and every sensory attribute examined. This affords a sound nutritional justification, in addition to the cultural and aromatic value already recognised, for the continued cultivation and conservation of these landraces. Among them, Kalojira was the richest in the bioactive fractions, Gobindabhog carried the best mineral profile with the lowest phytate load, and Radhunipagal yielded the softest product with the highest iron and zinc.
585: Fortification with beet extract raised total phenol approximately threefold, antioxidant activity approximately twofold and calcium approximately sixfold, and constituted the sole source of anthocyanin, while fortification with carrot extract constituted the sole source of beta-carotene and yielded the highest resistant starch with the lowest predicted glycaemic index. Both treatments softened the product, improved its colour and raised its acceptability, and did so to an equal extent in every variety. The gain in minerals is, however, partly offset by an accompanying rise in phytate, so that the phytate to mineral ratio rather than the mineral content alone should be used in judging the nutritional value of the fortified product.
586: On the basis of overall performance, KBI, namely idli prepared from Kalojira and fortified with beet extract, is recommended as the superior combination, having returned the highest total phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant activity, soluble protein, anthocyanin and overall acceptability. KCI is recommended where a provitamin A-rich product of low glycaemic response is required, and GBI where a mineral-enriched product is required. The plain product of the non-aromatic check was the poorest treatment for almost every character examined and is unsuited to this purpose.
587: The wider significance of these findings is that a traditional fermented food may be enriched in phenolics, antioxidants, provitamin A and minerals using nothing more than two commonly available vegetables, without recourse to any synthetic colourant, additive or fortificant, and without any loss of consumer acceptance. This affords a practical route for adding value to the aromatic rice landraces of West Bengal and for improving the nutritional quality of a food consumed daily by a large population.
588: Certain limitations should be recognised. The study was confined to four varieties and to a single level of fortification, and the sensory evaluation was conducted by a semi-trained panel rather than a consumer panel. The bioaccessibility of the added minerals and pigments was not determined directly, and the shelf life and microbiological stability of the fortified batter were not examined. Further work may therefore be directed towards optimising the level of vegetable extract, determining the in vitro bioaccessibility of the added iron, zinc and calcium in the presence of the observed phytate, characterising the individual phenolic acids and betalains by chromatographic methods, and evaluating the storage behaviour and consumer acceptance of the fortified product on a larger scale.
